outcomes.question: Before I put time into this: is it well regarded? Has it been criticised or superseded?
outcomes.text:
It's worth your time, and it's contested in useful ways. It won the 2025 Berggruen essay prize [spya-gp3g6s]. A search found replies, including Barton Friedland's critique in Noema, [a LinkedIn post discussing it](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/pevansgreenwood_the-consciences-debate-continues-in-noema-activity-7443091909155270656-CJZ2), and [Armando Vieira's Medium reply](https://medium.com/@Lidinwise/why-the-mythology-of-conscious-ai-misses-the-deeper-point-437589461d45). I found nothing saying it has been superseded.

Which would suit your group better: debating his arguments, or the ethics?

outcomes.question: What should I read before or alongside this to get the most out of it?
outcomes.text:
Read the essay first, then two critiques to argue with. [Ethics in Review](https://www.ethicsinreview.com/on-anil-seths-the-mythology-of-conscious-ai-part-1/) disputes how claims of existing conscious AI should be read. [Skygazing](https://skygazing.substack.com/p/you-look-like-a-thing-whats-wrong) says Seth doesn't examine what biology contributes. I only saw search summaries, not the full pages.

Seth's own pivot is "I’ve made a case against conscious AI, but I might be wrong" [spya-qu7j89].

Are you leading the discussion?

outcomes.question: Who is the author, and how far should I trust them on this subject?
outcomes.text:
Seth is a neuroscience professor who directs Sussex's Centre for Consciousness Science [spya-rg493b]. That's a strong credential on consciousness, though not on AI engineering. His view that life matters is a minority one. He says so himself [spya-qu7j89], and a [reviewer of his book](https://www.naturalism.org/resources/book-reviews/naturalizing-consciousness-review-of-being-you-by-anil-seth) disagrees. In his [later paper](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/behavioral-and-brain-sciences/article/conscious-artificial-intelligence-and-biological-naturalism/C9912A5BE9D806012E3C8B3AF612E39A) he concedes the stronger version is hard to defend.

Will your group be arguing for or against him?

outcomes.question: Before I put time into this: is it well regarded? Has it been criticised or superseded?
outcomes.text:
It's influential and contested. Gwern himself followed up in ["Scaling Hypothesis Revisited"](https://gwern.net/scaling-hypothesis-revisited), and an [outside piece](https://ain3xt.com/en/posts/20200528-the-scaling-hypothesis/) says he missed inference-time scaling. A [Hacker News thread](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=31564033) argues about plateaus. It's a 2020 essay, so read it as a dated, partisan argument.

Is your group discussing the scaling claim itself or the essay's rhetoric?

outcomes.question: What should I read before or alongside this to get the most out of it?
outcomes.text:
Read Kaplan et al.'s "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models" and Sutton's "The Bitter Lesson". Both are in [Gwern's scaling directory](https://gwern.net/doc/ai/scaling/index), and the essay leans on both [spya-sctj6d spya-sfkxh8]. Afterward, [Scaling Hypothesis Revisited](https://gwern.net/scaling-hypothesis-revisited) shows how the author's view changed.

Is your group more interested in the technical claims or the forecasting critique?

outcomes.question: Who is the author, and how far should I trust them on this subject?
outcomes.text:
Gwern is Gwern Branwen, an independent writer and researcher with no institutional affiliation, who [describes himself as freelance](https://gwern.net/me). He's a respected, well-read voice on scaling, but he writes as an advocate. Weigh his strongest claims accordingly. For a reading group, the open question is whether the strong claim can be tested. One [philosophy-of-science paper](https://philsci-archive.pitt.edu/23622/1/psa_scaling_hypothesis_manuscript.pdf) argues it can't be.

Which would your group rather dig into: the technical argument or the forecasts?
